##Part A
```{r}
m1 <- matrix(1:9, nrow = 3, ncol = 3)
m1

m2 <- matrix(1:9, nrow = 3, ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)
m2

scores <- matrix(c(88, 92, 79, 95, 84, 90), nrow = 2, ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)
rownames(scores) <- c("Quiz1", "Quiz2")
colnames(scores) <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid")
scores

## Q1 By default, R fills a matrix column by column m1. With byrow = TRUE, it fills row by row m2. Same numbers, different order

## Q2 R still makes the matrix but gives a warning. It recycles the first value (1) to fill the 9th slot, and warns because 8 is not a multiple of 8 rows.

##PART B
scores[1, 2]
scores[1, ]
scores[, "Ben"]
scores

scores[scores >= 90]

class(scores[1, ])
class(scores[, "Ben"])

##Q4: A logical condition picks out individual values wherever they are in the matrix so the result can't keep the rows and columns. R returns just those values as a plain vector, with no row or column names.

##PART C
dim(scores)
nrow(scores)
ncol(scores)

scores_t <- t(scores)
scores_t 
dim(scores_t)
dim(scores)

a <- matrix(1:4, nrow = 2)
b <- matrix(5:8, nrow = 2)

a + b
a * b

a %% b

##Q5: a * b multiplies matching positions which is 1x5 and 3x7. a%%b is true matrix multiplication rows of a times columns of b then summed
##6: dim(scores) is 23 and dim(scores_t) is 32. The names swap too because the rows before the columns, so the labels must follow their data

##PART D 
scores_v2 <- cbind(scores, Dex = c(85, 91))
scores_v2

scores_v3 <- rbind(scores, Quiz3 = c(80, 88, 93))
scores_v3

cbind(scores, c(85, 91, 100))

##PART E
arr <- array(1:12, dim = c(2, 3, 2))
arr

arr[1, 2, 2]
arr[, , 1]
dim(arr)

##Q9: dim(arr) gives 2 3 2: 2 rows, 3 columns, and 2 stacked layers
##Q10: daily temperature readings of 3 cities, taken at 4 times a day, over 2 days. Rows are times, columns are cities, and layers are days
##11: One 2D matrix can only hold a single day, so a third dimension is needed to keep everyday together.

##PART F
class_a <- matrix(c(85, 90, 78, 92), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE,
                  dimnames = list(c("S1", "S2"), c("Midterm", "Final")))
class_b <- matrix(c(88, 84, 95, 91), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE,
                  dimnames = list(c("S3", "S4"), c("Midterm", "Final")))

all_students <- rbind(class_a, class_b)
all_students
rowMeans(all_students)

##Q11: I chose rbind() because the classes have different students(S1, S2 vs S3, S4,)but the same columns (Midterm, Final). New students mean new rows. Shared column names were the clue.
##Q12: Stack all 5 matrices with rbind(), since they share the same 2 columns, Then check dim(): columns should be 2, and rows should equal the total students from all 5 classes.

##Conclusion: A matrix is a 2D table ([row, col]), while an array adds more dimensions by stacking layers ([row, col, layer]). Both hold one data type. In a student dataset, rbind() adds new students as rows, and cbind() adds a new score column like a Final exam.
